info.bio:
Louis Jordan (Brinkley,08 de Junio de 1908-04de Febrero de 1975),saxofonista y cantante Estadounidense de Blues,fue uno de los pioneros del Jazz y del Rhythm and Blues.

Su padre líder de la orquesta Rabbit Foot Minstrels,le enseñó a tocar el saxo y siendo adolescente le permitió que se uniese a la misma orquesta durante los veranos.Más tarde,tocaría también con otras orquestas como las "Ma Rainey" y "Kaiser Marshall".

En 1932 se instala en Filadelfia y se une a la orquesta de Charlie Gaines.

scenes.name: El Renacimiento de Harlem y el swing
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Inspirado por el nacionalismo negro de Marcus Garvey («Up you mighty race!»), el Renacimiento de Harlem buscó la sofisticación frente a los estereotipos racistas, con una casta interna (ciudad contra campo, claros contra oscuros) que miraba por encima del hombro el blues rural, es decir, lo funky. Cab Calloway y luego Louis Jordan encarnaron al líder de banda que se mueve al compás y rapea percusivamente. El swing de los treinta, orquestado y estructurado, se alejó de sus raíces hasta que los blancos lo tocaron igual: Benny Goodman y Paul Whiteman se llevaron el dinero, y Ted Vincent lo llama «el disco de los años treinta».

scenes.name: Rhythm and blues
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: En los cuarenta, los combos de jump como el Tympany Five de Louis Jordan sustituyeron a las big bands: baile, ritmo, scat, solo de saxo. Gente que trabajaba duro todo el día necesitaba música fuerte y con alma: un grito sincero, un saxo, una guitarra rockera. Su «misma vulgaridad», dice LeRoi Jones, aseguraba su conexión con la vida de la gente, y esa vulgaridad fue el ingrediente principal del funk. Despreciado por los intelectuales como mal jazz, el R&B dio a Chuck Berry, Little Richard y Bo Diddley, inspiró el rock and roll y la invasión británica, y en el chitlin circuit fue el útero del funk. Con Live at the Apollo de James Brown (1962, disco de oro) el R&B se hizo mayor; de él salieron Ray Charles, Brown y Aretha Franklin.

scenes.name: Antecedentes (1892-1950)
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Antes del rock'n'roll: Tin Pan Alley, los primeros discos de blues (Mamie Smith) y de «old-time music», el yodel de Jimmie Rodgers, el crooning de Bing Crosby, el boogie-woogie, el jump blues de Louis Jordan (nacimiento de facto del rhythm'n'blues), la guitarra jazzística de T-Bone Walker, Woody Guthrie como primer gran cantautor y la exótica de Les Baxter. En paralelo, la vanguardia clásica (Russolo, Satie, Varèse, Cage, Schaeffer) anticipa el ruido, el ambient y la electrónica.

podcast.title: Alternating Pianists with Wild Bill Davis
podcast.body: While officially Bill Doggett joined Louis Jordan in 1949, interviews suggest he joined much earlier, alternating with Jordan's other piano player, Wild Bill Davis. According to Bill Adams, involved in Jordan's management, Davis would tour for a week while Doggett arranged, and then they would swap roles. "But I've seen interviews with members of Jordan's organisation that suggest he joined much earlier, but he would alternate with Jordan's other piano player, Wild Bill Davis."

podcast.title: Attempt to Poach Band Members and Firing
podcast.body: Convinced of his and Ella Fitzgerald's importance to Chick Webb's band, Louis Jordan planned to form his own group, taking Ella and other members with him. Webb discovered the plan and fired Jordan, while most of the band, including Ella, remained loyal. "He thought that he and Ella were the two important ones in the web band, and he planned to form his own band, and take her, and much of the rest of the band, with him, web found out and fired Jordan, and Ella most of the band remained loyal to Webb."

podcast.title: Collaborations with Ella Fitzgerald
podcast.body: Louis Jordan had recorded hits with Ella Fitzgerald, a collaboration that began when they first worked together in Chick Webb's band in the 1930s. "just like the ink spots, he'd had hits to wedding with Ella Fitzgerald, who he'd first worked with back in the 1930s in Chick Webb's band."

podcast.title: Crossover Appeal and Country Market
podcast.body: Louis Jordan's music had crossover success, appealing to audiences of both Bob Wills and Big Joe Turner. This led him to record songs, like "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie," originally targeted at the white country market. "to appeal to the same audience that was listening to Bob Will's, just as much as you were to the audience that was listening to Big Joe Turner, and because of this crossover success, Jordan started recording occasional songs that were originally aimed at the white country market."

podcast.title: Exceptional Performer and Charisma
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was an exceptional performer capable of selling songs with wit, humor, and a hip-ness rivaled only by Cab Calloway and Slim Gaylord at the time. He was also a superior musician, charming, funny, tuneful, and attractive. "He was someone who could absolutely sell a song, with wit and humour, and a general sense of hip-ness that could possibly be matched at that time, only by Cap Calaway and Slim Gaylord."

podcast.title: First Studio Recordings with Tympany Five
podcast.body: On December 20, 1938, Louis Jordan and his "Alksrande v. band" (which soon became Louis Jordan and His Tympany Five) made their first studio recordings, laying down "Honey in the Bee Bowl" and "Barnacle Bill the Sailor." "on December 20, 1938, ten days before Roll and Pete was recorded, Louis Jordan and his Alksrande v. band went into the studio for the first time, to record Honey in the Bee Bowl, and Barnacle Bill the Sailor."

podcast.title: Formation of Tympany Five
podcast.body: After being fired from Chick Webb's band, Louis Jordan formed a smaller group called the Tympany Five (initially "Alksrande v. band"), drawing members from Jesse Stone's band. "As it was, instead, he formed a much smaller group, the Alksrande v. band, made up of members of Jesse Stone's band."

podcast.title: Frontman Role in Chick Webb's Band
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was a crucial alto sax player and male lead vocalist for Chick Webb's band, often taking on the frontman role. He was so integral that some people mistakenly thought he was Chick Webb himself. "This sax player did a lot of the frontman job for Webb's band, and he was so important to the band in those years, that allegedly, some people thought he was Chick Webb."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Fusion of Genres in "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie"
podcast.body: Jordan's "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" exemplified a fusion of genres, resembling Bob Wills' Western Swing (lacking only fiddle or steel guitar) while clearly showcasing the horn-driven pulse and hip, jive vocals characteristic of rhythm and blues, making it a seminal example of early rock and roll. "There's only really the lack of a fiddle or steel guitar to distinguish the styles, but you can also hear the horn driven pulse and the hip vocals that characterize rhythm and blues."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Inspired by Hampton's Band
podcast.body: Musicians such as Louis Jordan were clearly inspired by Lionel Hampton's band, which pioneered Jump band music that eventually became known as rhythm and blues. This demonstrates the direct lineage from Hampton's innovations to future R&B stars. "and musicians such as Louis Jordan were clearly inspired by Hampton's band."

podcast.title: Jamaican Taste Preference (1960s)
podcast.body: Even as American musical tastes shifted towards rock and pop in the early 1960s, Jamaican audiences continued to prefer the R&B and Jump Band sounds of artists like Louis Jordan. "Jamaican audiences wanted Louis Jordan, Fat Storner and Jean and Eunice, but the Americans wanted Elvis and Gerrilly Lewis and Bobby Daring."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 114: "My Boy Lollipop" by Millie

podcast.title: James Brown's Idol
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was James Brown's ultimate musical idol and the artist Brown tried to emulate more than any other. Brown, as a child, listened to Jordan's records on the radio and saw him in film shorts, which inspired his own aspirations to perform. "But his real favourite, the one he tried to emulate more than any other, was Louis Jordan."

podcast.body: Louis Jordan's jive singing style was used as a point of comparison for Wynonie Harris's more subtle vocal performances. "close to the give singing of a cap-caller way or Louis Jordan."

podcast.title: Late Career Recordings
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was among the artists whose late-career recordings were released by Johnny Otis's Blues Spectrum Records in the 1970s. Some of these recordings were Jordan's last ever. "He ran blues spectrum records in the 70s, which put out late career recordings by people like Charles Brown, Big Joe Turner and Louis Jordan. Some of them their last ever recordings"

podcast.title: Little Richard's Foremost Musical Inspiration
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was considered Little Richard's single biggest musical inspiration, and his recording of "Keep a-Knockin'" directly prompted Richard to record his own version of the song. "Jordan was, of course, Richard's single biggest musical inspiration, so we can reasonably assume that the record by Jordan was the one that pushed him to record the song."

srcs.episode: Episode 54: Keep A Knockin

podcast.title: Male Jump Band Artist Typically Covered by Country Musicians
podcast.body: Louis Jordan is noted as an example of a male jump band artist whose R&B music was more commonly covered by country musicians who ventured into R&B, unlike the jazz-influenced female artists Janice Martin preferred. "performing music originally recorded by male jump band artists like Louis Jordan."

podcast.title: Managed by Mo Gale
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was one of the artists managed by Mo Gale, who also oversaw the careers of Lucky Millinder, Sister Rosetta Tharpe, The Ink Spots, and Ella Fitzgerald. "Jordan was another act in Mo Gale's stable."

podcast.title: Most Popular R&B Group Leader
podcast.body: Louis Jordan led the most popular R&B group in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and his work inspired a wide range of artists, including Chuck Berry and Bill Haley. "He was also, as you may remember from earlier episodes, the leader of the most popular Arwenby group in the late 40s and early 50s."

podcast.title: Peak Commercial Success with Bill Doggett
podcast.body: Bill Doggett joined Louis Jordan's band during its period of highest commercial success, serving as a key musical director and pianist. "Dogget was in Jordan's band during its period of peak commercial success."

podcast.title: Pivotal Influence on Early Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Louis Jordan's 1940s records and style were widely emulated by nearly every musician during the early rock and roll period, making him a foundational figure for the genre. "Essentially, every musician in the early rock and roll period was to a greater or less of extent copying the style of Louis Jordan's 1940s records"

podcast.body: Mickey Baker contributed to records by Louis Jordan, showcasing his versatility as a studio musician. "And records by Louis Jordan, LeVern Baker, Ray Charles and Moore."

podcast.title: Sound System Favorite
podcast.body: Louis Jordan was a significant favorite among the early Jamaican sound system audiences, whose music formed a bulk of what was played for dancing. "Louis Jordan was a big favourite."

podcast.title: Success through Jive Singing in Jump Band Music
podcast.body: Louis Jordan's jive singing style was instrumental to the success of jump band music, as this stripped-down genre relied heavily on vocal personality to provide the character that would otherwise come from more instruments in larger bands. "His jive singing style gives the music all the character that in the larger bands would be conveyed by other instruments"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 4: "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" by Louis Jordan

podcast.title: Unique Stage Personality and Vocal Style
podcast.body: Louis Jordan combined the jump band sound with his unique stage personality and highly expressive vocal style, which was characterized by "putting personality into his vocals." He was part of the jive singing tradition, known for being hip, clever, funny, sophisticated, and using made-up words or singing about taboo subjects. "But what he was very good at was putting personality into his vocals."
